@graph.name: Yuzu Kosho Edamame
@graph.description: Tender edamame pods marinated in citrusy ponzu and zesty yuzu kosho. It’s an effortless 3-ingredient snack with a bright flavor and a subtle kick of heat.
recipeIngredient: 14 oz unshelled edamame ((1 package; boiled or thawed according to package instructions))
2 tsp yuzu kosho (Japanese citrus chili paste)

itemListElement.text: If using edamame pods, snip off the tips of each pod with kitchen shears to help the marinade absorb better. Skip this step if using shelled edamame.Nami's Tip: This allows the marinade to seep directly inside to the beans.
itemListElement.name: If using edamame pods, snip off the tips of each pod with kitchen shears to help the marinade absorb better. Skip this step if using shelled edamame.Nami's Tip: This allows the marinade to seep directly inside to the beans.

itemListElement.text: In a prep tray or resealable plastic bag, whisk together ponzu, water, and yuzu kosho until the paste is fully dissolved.Nami's Tip: Taste the mixture and adjust the flavor to your liking; it should taste slightly stronger so it penetrates the edamame well.

itemListElement.text: Add the edamame to the prep tray (or the bag), cover (or seal the bag), and shake or toss until thoroughly coated.

itemListElement.text: Refrigerate for at least 2 hours (or overnight for maximum flavor), shaking or tossing occasionally.

itemListElement.text: Toss once more before serving and finish with salt if desired (especially if your edamame was not salted).

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, as long as your ponzu is vegan. Traditional ponzu contains katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes), so check the label.
It has a noticeable but gentle kick. Yuzu kosho tastes bright and tangy rather than fiery. Use less for a milder version.

@graph.name: Where can I buy yuzu kosho?

acceptedAnswer.text: Japanese grocery stores like Mitsuwa and Nijiya stock it in the condiments section. It's also sold online and at Trader Joe's. See my full yuzu kosho pantry guide for more info.
